original_description: Catch the failures that survive every per-item check — a script where each sentence is faithful to its source and the ORDER asserts something no sentence says; a shot whose image and caption are each true and whose PAIRING claims a third thing; an ending whose FORM contradicts the thesis. Use this whenever writing, cutting, reordering or reviewing a narration or voiceover script; whenever deciding what a shot shows under a given line; whenever trimming for length, because cutting a premise leaves its conclusion standing and nothing goes red; when choosing how a piece opens or ends; and before recording or locking a cut. Reach for it especially when every gate is green and the piece still feels wrong, or when a reader says "this doesn't follow" and the sentences all check out — that is the signature of a relational failure, because fidelity checking reads each claim alone.
best_description: Use this when the question is about how the parts of a film or script relate, not whether each part is accurate: where a line sits and what its position implies; whether moving, reordering, opening or ending with something changes what the piece argues; whether repeated lines are emphasis or padding; whether a trim left a conclusion without its premise; whether a shot and the words over it assert a third thing neither says; whether the ending's shape fits the thesis. Reach for it in any narration or voiceover work — drafting, cutting to length, resequencing, pairing shots to lines, reviewing before recording or locking — and especially when a line "doesn't land", a reader says "this doesn't follow", or every fidelity check passes and the piece still feels wrong. Per-sentence source checks read each claim alone and cannot see any of this.
final_description: Use this for any question about what a film or script implies by its arrangement, not whether its facts are right. Reach for it when: moving, reordering, opening with or ending on a line, and asking what that position asserts; worrying an order suggests a cause, motive or intention nobody stated; trimming to length and wondering what the surviving lines still refer to; repeated lines that may be emphasis or padding; choosing which image sits under which narration, and what the pair claims together; whether an ending's shape fits the argument. Applies while drafting an opening, resequencing, cutting to time, pairing shots to lines, or reviewing before recording or locking — and whenever a line "doesn't land", someone says "this doesn't follow", or every source check passes and the piece still feels wrong. Not for fact-checking, proofreading, captions, rendering or code: those read each item alone and are blind to all of this.
